kurals.tamil:
வேண்டற்க வென்றிடினும் சூதினை வென்றதூஉம்
தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Vendarka vendridinum soodhinai vendradhooum
thoondirpon meenvizhungi atru.
kurals.meaning: Do not desire gambling even if you are able to win, because the winnings are like the bait a fish swallows along with the iron hook hidden inside it.
kurals.elementary: A fish sees a tasty worm and gulps it, happy for one second, but the worm hides a sharp hook. Valluvar says winning at gambling is that worm: it feels like a prize, but it pulls you in and you cannot get away.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by closing the most tempting loophole: vendridinum (வென்றிடினும், 'even should you win') concedes the gambler's best case and still forbids the desire (vendarka, வேண்டற்க). The simile turns on thoondirpon (தூண்டிற்பொன்), where pon (பொன்), usually 'gold', is read by the commentators as 'metal, iron': Mu. Varadarasanar on both ytamizh and thirukkural.net glosses it as தூண்டில் இரும்பு, 'the iron of the hook', and Kalaignar speaks of the iron barb (இரும்பு முள்). The alapedai in vendradhooum (வென்றதூஉம்) gives emphasis: even the thing won. The tradition descending from Parimelazhagar reads this chapter, like the two before it (Varaivin Magalir and Kallunnaamai), as a list of pleasures a ruler and a householder must shun, and the opening couplet sets the theme that gambling's gains are themselves the trap. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Dice, verily, are armed with goads and driving-hooks, deceiving and tormenting, causing grievous woe. They give frail gifts and then destroy the man who wins, thickly anointed with the player's fairest good.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Vedic Gambler's Hymn the speaker describes dice as hooked weapons that hand out small gifts only to ruin even the winner.
hinduism.tie_back: The hymn's hooks that destroy the man who wins match the Kural's hook hidden in the fish's bait.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.7 (Gambler's Hymn), trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the hook imagery and the ruin of the winner are a near one-to-one match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain is worth if it costs a person their very self.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a win can be a loss in disguise.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; same logic of a ruinous gain, but the verse is not about gambling.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an admits that gambling can bring some gain but judges the harm to be greater.
islam.tie_back: Both texts grant that one may win and still say: do not want it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; directly weighs the winnings against the harm, as the Kural does.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And as an asmakhta does not effect acquisition, the one who wins takes money that is not legally his, and is considered a robber.”
judaism.explanation: In the Talmud, Rami bar Hama argues that a dice-player's winnings are not truly his, so even the winner counts as a kind of robber.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud, like the Kural, denies that the gambler's win is a real gain.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria, including Steinsaltz's explanatory words; the argument is legal rather than moral-psychological.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He bolts the die quite boldly,--knowing not / What burning poison thereon lurks unseen.”
buddhism.explanation: In this Jataka a cheating dice-player keeps swallowing a die to escape losing, not knowing the Bodhisatta has coated the dice with poison.
buddhism.tie_back: A gambler swallowing what hides poison is close to the Kural's fish swallowing what hides a hook.
buddhism.source: Litta Jataka (No. 91), The Jataka vol. I, ed. E. B. Cowell
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the swallowing image is a striking match, though the Jataka's frame lesson is about using requisites thoughtlessly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...because by a sad spite I had killed the son of Amphidamas- not of set purpose, but in childish quarrel over the dice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The ghost of Patroclus recalls that a boyhood quarrel over dice made him a killer and sent him into exile.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A small game that seemed harmless carried a hidden cost, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; shows dice leading to ruin, but says nothing about the danger of winning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But the gamester and the footpad (and the highwayman) belong to the class of the mean, since they have a sordid love of gain.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle classes the gambler with the robber because both love gain from the wrong source.
philosophy.tie_back: For Aristotle, as for Valluvar, even successful gambling gains are something not worth wanting.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Classics Archive; condemns the gambler's gain but has no image of a trap.

kurals.tamil:
ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்க்கும் உண்டாங்கொல்
நன்றெய்தி வாழ்வதோர் ஆறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ondreydhi noorizhakkum soodharkkum undaangol
nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru.
kurals.meaning: Gamblers gain one and lose a hundred; can there ever be, for such people, a way of living that reaches anything good?
kurals.elementary: Imagine trading a hundred of your marbles for the chance to win one. You would soon have none left. Valluvar asks: if someone keeps doing that, how could life ever go well for them?
kurals.university: The couplet works through a stark ratio, ondreydhi noorizhakkum (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும், 'gaining one, losing a hundred'), and then a rhetorical question ending in -kol (உண்டாங்கொல், 'will there be?'), which expects the answer no. Soodhar (சூதர்) means gamblers; aaru (ஆறு) is 'way, path', so nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru is 'a path of living that attains good'. The particle -um in soodharkkum ('even for gamblers') implies that other sinners may still find such a path, but gamblers, as a class, are shut out. Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net softens the arithmetic to 'losing by hundreds out of the hope of gain', and Kalaignar reads it psychologically: a single win lures the player on into a hundred losses. Both base-text sites agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As of a costly horse grown old and feeble, I find not any profit of the gamester.”
hinduism.explanation: The repentant gambler of the Rig Veda admits his habit has yielded no profit, only decline.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say the gambler's way of life never arrives at any good.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.3, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; same verdict of no lasting profit, without the one-versus-hundred image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a craving to get rich leads people into traps that end in ruin.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, chasing one gain, is the person who falls into this snare.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; about greed generally, not gambling in particular.

islam.quote_or_event: “...In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets the small benefit of gambling against its much larger harm.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's one-gained-hundred-lost reckoning in moral terms.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; close match to the lopsided balance of gain and loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wealth may dwindle to less than nothing, / But one who gathers little by little increases it.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts wealth that vanishes with wealth built slowly through steady effort.
judaism.tie_back: The gambler's path leads to nothing, while the patient path the Kural implies leads to a good life.
judaism.source: Proverbs 13:11 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; this translation does not name gambling, though the verse is often applied to quick gains.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are, young householder, these six evil consequences in indulging in gambling: (i) the winner begets hate, (ii) the loser grieves for lost wealth, (iii) loss of wealth...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists what gambling brings: hatred if you win, grief and loss if you lose.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that neither winning nor losing gives the gambler a good life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a direct teaching on gambling's net loss.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Patroclus, as a boy, killed a playmate in a quarrel over dice and had to leave his home for exile at the house of Peleus.
greek_mythology.explanation: One small game cost Patroclus his home and set the course of his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A tiny stake leading to a huge loss echoes the Kural's one gained, a hundred lost.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Episode verified in Butler's text; it is a loose fit, since no stake or winnings are involved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Both, then, since they are willing to make gain from wrong sources, are sordid lovers of gain...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gambler and the robber both look for gain where it should not be sought.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks whether such a source of gain can ever lead to a good life, and Aristotle answers no.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a moral judgment rather than an account of net loss.

kurals.tamil:
உருளாயம் ஓவாது கூறின் பொருளாயம்
போஒய்ப் புறமே படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Urulaayam oovaadhu koorin porulaayam
pooip purame padum.
kurals.meaning: If a person keeps endlessly calling out stakes on the rolling dice, his wealth and the income that sustains it will leave him and fall into the hands of others.
kurals.elementary: A king who spends all day shouting bets at a dice board has no time left to look after his kingdom. Little by little, his treasure and his lands end up in other people's hands.
kurals.university: The couplet plays two compounds against each other: urulaayam (உருளாயம், 'gain from what rolls', i.e. the die, கவறு) and porulaayam (பொருளாயம், 'wealth and its revenue'). Oovaadhu koorin (ஓவாது கூறின்) means 'if one ceaselessly calls', which Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar take as calling out the stake, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as boasting of one's winnings. Pooip (போஒய், alapedai of போய்) purame padum says the wealth 'goes and lands outside', which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss as 'reaches the enemies' (பகைவர்). Pope's English ('If prince unceasing speak of nought but play') and his prose gloss follow the traditional Parimelazhagar reading, which takes the subject to be a king, in keeping with the chapter's place in Porutpaal. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira plays dice against Shakuni, staking and losing his treasury, his kingdom and finally his brothers to Duryodhana.
hinduism.explanation: A righteous king who could not stop calling out stakes handed his whole realm to his rivals in one sitting.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's picture of a king's wealth and revenue passing to his enemies.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (dice-game episode), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known episode summarised in plain prose; a near-exact narrative illustration.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, the prodigal son quickly squanders the property his father gave him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's gambler, he lets his wealth drain away into others' hands.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; about general dissipation, not gambling specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands believers to avoid gambling so that they can prosper.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse case: a ruler who will not avoid it loses his wealth.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (the translation's own spelling 'alters' kept); the prohibition matches, but it says nothing about wealth passing to others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...those who play dice are disqualified because they are not involved in settling the world, i.e., in productive occupations that demand hard work.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Sheshet says the habitual dice-player is not trusted because he contributes nothing to the productive life of society.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's player who does nothing but call stakes earns nothing, so his income drains away.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, including Steinsaltz's explanatory gloss; the link is the gambler's unproductiveness, not loss to enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who brings ruin be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: ... (iv) he is a companion in indulging in gambling which causes heedlessness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that a gambling companion is really an enemy dressed up as a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's gambler likewise ends up handing his wealth to the very people across the board from him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; links gambling with ruin by hostile parties, but more loosely than the Kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The Athenians from the city had just finished their midday meal, after which they had betaken themselves, some to dice, others to sleep, when Pisistratus with his troops fell upon them and put them to the rout.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus tells how Athens fell to Pisistratus while its defenders were busy at dice and napping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A city lost to a rival while its men played dice is the Kural's warning on a political scale.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; this is history-legend rather than myth, and dice are one distraction among others.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The king is surrounded by persons whose only thought is to divert the king, and to prevent his thinking of self.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal notes that kings are kept in constant play and amusement so they never stop to reflect.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's king, endlessly calling dice, is the diverted ruler who loses track of his realm.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; about diversion in general, with no direct claim about loss of wealth.

kurals.tamil:
சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும் சூதின்
வறுமை தருவதொன்று இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirumai palaseydhu seerazhikkum soodhin
varumai tharuvadhondru il.
kurals.meaning: Nothing brings poverty like gambling, which causes many miseries and destroys a person's good name.
kurals.elementary: Some bad habits make you a little poorer. Gambling is the champion of them all: it takes your money, gets you into trouble, and makes people stop trusting you.
kurals.university: Sirumai pala seydhu (சிறுமை பல செய்து) means 'causing many miseries' (Mu. Varadarasanar: துன்பம் பலவற்றையும்), though sirumai literally means 'smallness, meanness' and can also suggest degradation. Seer (சீர்) here is renown or good standing, glossed as புகழ் by all four commentators. The superlative construction soodhin ... ondru il ('there is nothing like gambling') makes gambling the paramount cause of varumai (வறுமை, poverty). Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the verb as சீரழக்கும், but ytamizh's own transliteration ('seerazhikkum') and every gloss (கெடுக்கும், அழிக்கும்) support the standard சீரழிக்கும், so சீரழக்கும் looks like a shared typographical slip; this reading should be confirmed against a printed edition. Kesikan's gloss adds that gambling does this 'to those who love it' (தன்னை விரும்பியவருக்கு).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The gambler's wife is left forlorn and wretched: the mother mourns the son who wanders homeless. In constant fear, in debt, and seeking riches, he goes by night unto the home of others.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gambler's Hymn describes the gambler sinking into debt, homelessness and disgrace, dragging his family down with him.
hinduism.tie_back: It is a vivid picture of the poverty and lost good name the Kural attributes to gambling.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.10, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it combines poverty, misery and disgrace as the Kural does.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.”
christianity.explanation: Having wasted everything, the prodigal son falls into real poverty.
christianity.tie_back: This is the want that the Kural says gambling, above everything else, brings.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; poverty through squandering, though not specifically through gambling.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who played Nardashir (a game similar to backgammon) is like one who dyed his hand with the flesh and blood of swine.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares playing this game of chance to defiling one's hand with something forbidden.
islam.tie_back: The hadith matches the Kural's sense that gambling degrades a person's standing.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (the parenthetical is the translator's); a strong condemnation, but it says nothing about poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And these on the following list are the ones who are disqualified by the Sages from bearing witness due to their unseemly behavior...: One who plays with dice [bekubbiyya] for money...”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah strips the habitual dice-player of the right to testify, a public loss of standing.
judaism.tie_back: The gambler's lost credibility is the Kural's seer azhikkum, the ruin of good name.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:3 as given in Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, with an ellipsis over Steinsaltz's gloss; matches the loss of reputation but not the poverty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(iii) loss of wealth, (iv) his word is not relied upon in a court of law, (v) he is despised by his friends and associates...”
buddhism.explanation: Among the six evils of gambling, the Buddha names lost wealth, lost credibility and lost respect.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's double damage of poverty and ruined reputation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near point-by-point match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After the boy Patroclus killed a playmate in a quarrel over dice, his father Menoetius had to bring him away from Opoeis to live as an exile in the house of Peleus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A game of dice cost the young Patroclus his home and standing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows gambling causing misery and loss of place, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Episode verified in Butler's text; there is no poverty here, only exile and disgrace.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For it is for gain that both of them ply their craft and endure the disgrace of it...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gambler and the thief accept public disgrace for the sake of profit.
philosophy.tie_back: The disgrace Aristotle names is the Kural's ruined reputation.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it covers the disgrace but not the poverty.

kurals.tamil:
கவறும் கழகமும் கையும் தருக்கி
இவறியார் இல்லாகி யார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kavarum kazhagamum kaiyum tharukki
ivariyaar illaagi yaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who took pride in the dice, the gaming hall and their own skill of hand, and would not let them go, are the ones who have ended up with nothing.
kurals.elementary: Some people are very proud of being good at a game, and they love the place where it is played. But if that game is gambling and they never stop, Valluvar says, they finish with empty pockets, as many before them did.
kurals.university: The first line names gambling's three parts: kavaru (கவறு, the dice), kazhagam (கழகம், the gaming hall) and kai (கை, the hand, meaning dexterity in throwing). Tharukki (தருக்கி) means 'taking pride in', and ivariyaar (இவறியார்) means 'those who clung to, would not let go'. Illaagiyaar (இல்லாகியார்) is past tense: 'became people who have nothing'. Pope's English brings this out ('the men in other days who came to nought'), and Solomon Pappaiah adds that this 'has happened before too' (முன்பும் உண்டு), so the couplet appeals to historical examples. Kesikan reads it as 'those once wealthy and now destitute', and Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the parenthetical 'even though they had every wealth'. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net prints the dice as சுவறு, apparently a misprint for கவறு; the couplet itself is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Nalopakhyana of the Mahabharata, King Nala, possessed by Kali, keeps gambling against his brother Pushkara despite his queen's pleas, and loses his entire kingdom and wealth.
hinduism.explanation: A famous and accomplished king clung to the dice until he was left with nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: Nala is a classic case of the Kural's 'those who clung to dice in former days and came to nothing'.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana, trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known episode summarised in plain prose; the Kural's past-tense appeal fits such stories, though no commentator's naming of Nala was verified here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be...”
christianity.explanation: At the foot of the cross, the soldiers gamble for Jesus' seamless coat.
christianity.tie_back: It shows how gambling's pull goes on even in the darkest place, the same clinging the Kural condemns.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it depicts gambling but not the gambler's ruin, so the match is weak.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and whoever says to his companion. ‘Come along, let us gamble’ must give alms (as an expiation).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that even inviting someone to gamble is a wrong that needs expiation.
islam.tie_back: Even the first eager step toward the gaming table that the Kural warns about is treated as a fault.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it addresses the appetite for gambling, not the resulting poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Yehuda said: When are the people listed above disqualified from bearing witness? It is when they have no occupation but this one.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah singles out those who make dice their whole trade and identity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, proud of his dice, his hall and his hand, has made gambling his only occupation.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:3 as given in Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis-free extract with bold markup removed); it matches the total attachment but not the destitution.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be a rake, a drunkard, a gambler, and to squander all one earns — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names gambling and squandering as a cause of a person's downfall.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's verdict that those devoted to gambling become people with nothing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a direct match on gambling and downfall.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Athena finds Penelope's suitors amusing themselves with board games before the doors of Odysseus' hall while they consume his estate; they refuse to leave and are finally destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitors cling to the hall, its games and its pleasures, and it costs them everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's gamblers, they would not let go of the hall and its play, and came to nothing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of the well-known scene, not checked line by line this session; the board games are incidental to their ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...and the one faces the greatest dangers for the sake of the booty, while the other makes gain from his friends, to whom he ought to be giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats gambling as a craft practised for gain at the expense of friends.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, proud of his 'hand', is practising exactly this craft.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it covers the craft but not the ending in destitution.

kurals.tamil:
அகடாரார் அல்லல் உழப்பர்சூ தென்னும்
முகடியான் மூடப்பட் டார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Agadaaraar allal uzhapparsoo thennum
mugadiyaan moodappat taar.
kurals.meaning: Those swallowed up by the goddess of misfortune called gambling will never have their bellies filled and will suffer many sorrows.
kurals.elementary: Picture a big dark cloud named 'Bad Luck' that swallows people whole. Once it has you, you never get enough to eat and troubles keep coming. Valluvar says gambling is that cloud.
kurals.university: Mugadi (முகடி) is Misfortune personified, the goddess known in Tamil as Moodevi or Jyeshtha (மூதேவி), the inauspicious elder sister of Lakshmi. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss it as மூதேவி, and Pope's verse renders it 'Misfortune's other name'. Moodappattaar (மூடப்பட்டார்) means 'those covered or engulfed', which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as 'swallowed' (விழுங்கப்பட்டவர்). Agadaaraar (அகடாரார்) is 'those whose belly (அகடு) is never filled', and allal uzhappar means 'will toil in affliction'. Following Parimelazhagar's two-world reading, Kesikan and the Pope prose gloss take the second clause to mean suffering in the next world as well. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net seems to drop the negation ('வயிறார உணவைப் பெறுவதுடன்'), which is likely a transcription slip. The couplet text matches on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sad is the gambler when he sees a matron, another's wife, and his well-ordered dwelling. He yokes the brown steeds in the early morning, and when the fire is cold sinks down an outcast.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic gambler, gripped by the dice, ends each day cold, homeless and outcast while others prosper.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the endless affliction the Kural says comes to those engulfed by gambling.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.11, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on misery, but it lacks the personified Misfortune and the image of hunger.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.”
christianity.explanation: The ruined prodigal son is so hungry he envies the pigs' food.
christianity.tie_back: His unfilled belly is almost word for word the Kural's agadaaraar.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the hunger image matches closely, though the cause is general waste rather than gambling.

islam.quote_or_event: “...intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan...”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents gambling as the work of a malign spiritual power.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's Mugadi, gambling is pictured as an evil force that takes hold of its victims.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, with the translation's 'alters' kept; it shares the idea of a malign agent, without the hunger.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lover of money is never satisfied with money, nor a lover of wealth, with income. That too is futile.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes that chasing money never brings satisfaction.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's gamblers whose bellies are never full show the same insatiable want.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (Hebrew numbering; JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the dissatisfaction here is about desire, not literal hunger or gambling.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who plays with dice and drinks intoxicants, goes to women who are dear unto others as their own lives, associates with the mean and not with elders — he declines just as the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's verse describes the dice-player steadily waning like the moon.
buddhism.tie_back: The waning moon slowly covered by darkness parallels the Kural's gambler covered by Misfortune.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a similar image of being engulfed, with gambling bundled with other vices.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus reports a Lydian tradition that during a long famine the Lydians invented dice and other games, playing on one day so as not to think of food and eating on the next.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend links the very origin of dice-games with hunger that could not be satisfied.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dice and an empty belly go together in both texts, though Herodotus treats the games as a way to cope rather than a cause.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Summarised from the well-known passage but not re-checked verbatim this session; the causal direction is reversed from the Kural's.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We do not seek that easy and peaceful lot which permits us to think of our unhappy condition, nor the dangers of war, nor the labour of office, but the bustle which averts these thoughts of ours, and amuses us.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal argues that people chase play and bustle to escape facing their own wretchedness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, covered by Misfortune, is trapped in this kind of distraction and never filled.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the psychology overlaps, but Pascal is not condemning gambling specifically.

kurals.tamil:
பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்
கழகத்துக் காலை புகின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhagiya selvamum panbum kedukkum
kazhagaththuk kaalai pugin.
kurals.meaning: If a person's time is spent in the gaming hall, it destroys both the wealth that has come down to him and his good character.
kurals.elementary: Your grandparents may have saved a treasure for your family and taught you good manners. Valluvar says that hanging around a gambling house can waste both: the treasure is lost, and the good manners slowly disappear too.
kurals.university: Pazhagiya selvam (பழகிய செல்வம்) is 'long-familiar wealth', which all commentators take as ancestral or inherited property (Kalaignar: மூதாதையர் தேடிவைத்த சொத்து). Panbu (பண்பு) is good character or natural virtue. The second line contains an interpretive crux: kaalai (காலை) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Kesikan as kaalam, 'time' ('if one's time is passed in the gaming hall'), and Kesikan adds 'the time meant for doing good'. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads it literally as 'morning' ('if one goes to the gaming hall in the morning'), the hour that should belong to work. Kazhagam (கழகம்) also appears in 935 as the gaming place. The couplet is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Drinking, dice, women, and hunting, these four (which have been enumerated) in succession, he must know to be the most pernicious in the set that springs from love of pleasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king that dice are among the four most destructive vices born of love of pleasure.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu's grouping (drink, dice, women) is the same as the Kural's sequence of chapters 92 to 94, and both warn that these destroy a ruler's estate and character.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts; it names the vice but does not describe inherited wealth being lost.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: The prodigal son takes his share of the family inheritance and wastes it in dissolute living.
christianity.tie_back: A squandered inheritance and a corrupted life are exactly what the Kural says the gaming hall produces.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the inheritance and character theme closely, though gambling is not named.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says gambling turns people away from prayer and remembrance of God, and sows hatred.
islam.tie_back: Time taken by the gaming hall is time stolen from virtue, as the Kural's kaalai reading suggests.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the theme of lost time and corrupted character, with no mention of inherited wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wealth may dwindle to less than nothing, / But one who gathers little by little increases it.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts wealth that dwindles away with wealth that grows through steady care.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's ancestral fortune, lost in the gaming hall, is wealth dwindling to nothing.
judaism.source: Proverbs 13:11 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a general maxim that does not mention gaming or character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What are the six channels for dissipating wealth which he does not pursue? ... (d) indulgence in gambling which causes heedlessness...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists gambling among the six channels through which a householder's wealth drains away.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts present gambling as a leak that empties a family's fortune and its virtue.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on wealth, with heedlessness standing for the decline of character.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope's suitors pass their days in Odysseus' hall playing board games and feasting, eating up the estate of his house until they are destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Day after day spent in idle play and feasting swallows a great household's inherited wealth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's warning about time spent in the gaming hall wasting ancestral wealth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-checked verbatim this session; the wealth wasted belongs to Odysseus, not to the players.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Not that there is in fact any happiness in them, or that men imagine true bliss to consist in money won at play, or in the hare which they hunt; we would not take these as a gift.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal says people go to gaming not for the money but to fill and escape their time.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's focus on time spent in the gaming hall picks up the same insight: the real cost is the life poured away.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it speaks to the use of time but not to the loss of wealth or character.

kurals.tamil:
பொருள்கெடுத்துப் பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ அருள்கெடுத்து
அல்லல் உழப்பிக்கும் சூது.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulkeduththup poimer koleei arulkeduththu
allal uzhappikkum soodhu.
kurals.meaning: Gambling destroys wealth, drives a person to lying, kills compassion, and makes him suffer in misery.
kurals.elementary: First gambling takes your money. Then you start fibbing to cover it up. Then you stop caring about other people. And at the end you are very unhappy. Valluvar lists these four steps like a staircase going down.
kurals.university: The couplet is a chain of four causative actions with gambling (soodhu, சூது) held back as the subject until the last word. Porul keduththu (பொருள்கெடுத்து) means 'ruining wealth'; poi mer koleei (பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ) means 'making one take up falsehood', where koleei is the causative alapedai form of kol ('take'); arul keduththu (அருள்கெடுத்து) means 'destroying compassion'. The last verb, uzhappikkum (உழப்பிக்கும், 'causes to toil in affliction'), is also causative. Arul, the compassion celebrated in Arattuppaal's chapter 25 (Aruludaimai), is the highest of the virtues lost. Kesikan follows the Parimelazhagar tradition in reading the misery as belonging to both worlds (இருமையும்), and the Pope prose gloss adds '(here and hereafter)'. Both base sites agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva, Yudhishthira, having lost his wealth, his brothers and himself at dice, stakes and loses Draupadi, who is then dragged into the assembly and humiliated while the court looks on.
hinduism.explanation: The dice game first takes the Pandavas' wealth and then pushes the players past every limit of compassion and decency.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's descent from lost wealth to lost compassion to deep misery.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (dice-game episode), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known episode summarised in plain prose; matches the Kural's sequence closely, though the falsehood belongs mainly to Shakuni's cheating.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says love of money leads people away from faith and into many sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: Losing faith and being 'pierced with many sorrows' parallels the Kural's loss of compassion and the misery that follows.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a similar moral descent, though it concerns greed rather than gambling as such.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer...”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says gambling breeds hatred between people and pulls them away from God.
islam.tie_back: Animosity replacing goodwill is the Kural's arul keduththu, the destruction of compassion.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on the moral corruption that gambling causes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Since they do not realize the effort required of most people to earn a living they might not be scrupulous about other people’s money, and their testimony cannot be relied upon.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmudic discussion explains why a dice-player's word cannot be trusted in court.
judaism.tie_back: The gambler's unreliable testimony is the Kural's poi mer koleei, the turn to falsehood.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (Steinsaltz's explanatory gloss on Rav Sheshet, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; this sentence is Steinsaltz's commentary woven into the translation, not the Talmud's own words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) the winner begets hate, (ii) the loser grieves for lost wealth, (iii) loss of wealth, (iv) his word is not relied upon in a court of law...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's list covers hatred, grief, loss of wealth and loss of credibility.
buddhism.tie_back: This covers nearly every step of the Kural's chain: wealth lost, truthfulness doubted, goodwill gone, and grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong item-by-item correspondence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...I had killed the son of Amphidamas- not of set purpose, but in childish quarrel over the dice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: For the boy Patroclus, a dice game turned into a quarrel and the quarrel into a killing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is gambling destroying compassion and bringing lasting sorrow, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it is strong on lost compassion and misery but silent on wealth and lying.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...the other makes gain from his friends, to whom he ought to be giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gambler takes from his friends when he ought to be generous to them.
philosophy.tie_back: Taking from friends where one should give is the Kural's arul keduththu, generosity turned upside down.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a precise match on the loss of benevolence.

kurals.tamil:
உடைசெல்வம் ஊண்ஒளி கல்விஎன்று ஐந்தும்
அடையாவாம் ஆயங் கொளின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Udaiselvam oon-oli kalvi-endru aindhum
adaiyaavaam aayang kolin.
kurals.meaning: If a person takes up gambling, these five will never reach him: clothing, wealth, food, renown and learning.
kurals.elementary: Think of five good things: clothes to wear, money, food, a good name, and learning. Valluvar says that if you make gambling your habit, all five walk away from you.
kurals.university: The couplet lists five goods: udai (உடை, clothing), selvam (செல்வம், wealth), oon (ஊண், food), oli (ஒளி, 'light', i.e. fame or renown) and kalvi (கல்வி, learning). Aayam (ஆயம்) here means gambling, and aayang kolin means 'if one takes it up'. Adaiyaavaam (அடையாவாம்) says these 'will not come to' him, so the stress is on goods that are never gained, not only goods lost. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan list the five in reverse order (fame, learning, wealth, food, clothing), presumably following Parimelazhagar's ranking from highest to lowest, while Pope keeps the Kural's order. Kesikan adds 'even if one does it thinking it mere sport' (வேடிக்கை), and Sivayogi Sivakumar takes oli as 'self-knowledge'. The text is the same on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Nala loses his kingdom at dice to Pushkara, he wanders into the forest with Damayanti wearing a single cloth; starving, he throws that garment over some birds to catch them, and they fly away with it, leaving him naked, hungry and without a kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: The gambler-king is stripped in turn of wealth, food, clothing and royal glory.
hinduism.tie_back: Nala's fall is almost a list of the Kural's five lost goods.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana, trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known episode summarised in plain prose; it covers four of the five goods (learning is not involved).

christianity.quote_or_event: “...They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things therefore the soldiers did.”
christianity.explanation: Soldiers gamble for the clothes of a condemned man.
christianity.tie_back: Clothing changing hands by lot echoes the first of the Kural's five losses, seen from the winners' side.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a weak, inverted parallel offered as the best available, since it depicts the gamblers, not the gambler's loss.

islam.quote_or_event: “...But their sin is greater than their benefit. And they ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘The excess [beyond needs].’”
islam.explanation: The verse condemns gambling and in the same breath teaches spending only what is beyond one's needs.
islam.tie_back: The contrast protects the basic needs, such as food and clothing, that the Kural says the gambler loses.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the link to the five goods is indirect.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rather, those who play dice are disqualified because they are not involved in settling the world, i.e., in productive occupations that demand hard work.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Sheshet sees the dice-player as someone outside productive life.
judaism.tie_back: Someone who produces nothing will not gain the food, clothing and wealth the Kural lists.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, including Steinsaltz's gloss; the five goods are implied rather than named.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(v) he is despised by his friends and associates, (vi) he is not sought after for matrimony; for people would say he is a gambler and is not fit to look after a wife.”
buddhism.explanation: The gambler loses respect and the chance of marriage, because people judge him unable to provide.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's lost renown (oli) and inability to secure basic goods.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on reputation and provision, but it does not mention learning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus relates that Pisistratus' army overran the Athenians while some of them had gone off to dice after their midday meal.
greek_mythology.explanation: Men at their dice lost their city and with it their freedom and standing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The loss of everything a citizen has echoes the Kural's sweeping list of goods that will not come.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Passage verified in Rawlinson; it is history rather than myth, and the parallel to the five goods is loose.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Both, then, since they are willing to make gain from wrong sources, are sordid lovers of gain; therefore all such forms of taking are mean.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle concludes that the gambler's way of getting is mean and dishonourable.
philosophy.tie_back: Such meanness rules out the renown (oli) that the Kural counts among the five goods.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it addresses honour only, not the other four goods.

kurals.tamil:
இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல் துன்பம்
உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Izhaththoruum kaadhalikkum soodhepol thunbam
uzhaththoruum kaadhatru uyir.
kurals.meaning: Just as gambling is loved all the more the more one loses at it, so the soul loves the body all the more the more it suffers.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever lost a game and immediately shouted, 'One more try!'? The more you lose, the more you want to play. Valluvar says life is like that too: even when it hurts, we hold on to it more tightly.
kurals.university: The closing couplet turns a psychological observation about gambling into a general statement about existence. Izhaththoruum (இழத்தொறூஉம்) and uzhaththoruum (உழத்தொறூஉம்), both with alapedai, mean 'every time one loses' and 'every time one suffers', placing loss and pain in parallel. Kaadhalikkum (காதலிக்கும், 'comes to love') and kaadhatru (காதற்று) carry the comparison. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Pope) read kaadhatru as kaadhal + atru, 'has love, is fond': the soul (uyir) loves the body more as it suffers, just as the gambler loves gambling more as he loses. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh instead splits it as kaadhal + atru 'without love', giving the opposite sense that the soul does not love suffering, and adds that gambling can lead to despair. Pappaiah reverses which half is the comparison. The text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When I resolve to play with these no longer, my friends depart from me and leave me lonely. When the brown dice, thrown on the board, have rattled, like a fond girl I seek the place of meeting.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic gambler confesses that however much he resolves to stop, the rattle of dice pulls him back like a lover to a meeting.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's gambler, who loves the game more with every loss, described in his own words.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.5, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; an almost exact portrait of compulsive love for the game.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes being pulled again and again toward what he knows harms him.
christianity.tie_back: The gambler who loses and keeps playing shows this same divided will.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it captures the compulsion but not gambling or the soul-and-body comparison.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an acknowledges the small benefit that makes gambling attractive while judging its harm greater.
islam.tie_back: That small benefit is the lure that keeps the Kural's gambler loving the game through every loss.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it explains the attraction but not the deepening attachment with loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lover of money is never satisfied with money, nor a lover of wealth, with income. That too is futile.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet notes that desire for money only grows and is never satisfied.
judaism.tie_back: Desire that feeds on itself is the Kural's gambler, whose love grows as he loses.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (Hebrew numbering; JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; insatiable desire matches, though the verse concerns wealth, not loss at play.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...the noble truth of the origination of stress: the craving that makes for further becoming — accompanied by passion & delight, relishing now here & now there — i.e., craving for sensual pleasure, craving for becoming, craving for non-becoming.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's Second Noble Truth names craving for continued existence (bhava-tanha) as what binds beings to suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's soul clinging ever harder to a suffering body is this craving for becoming.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match for the second (soul-and-body) half of the couplet, though not for gambling.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus reports a Lydian legend that during an eighteen-year famine the people kept up their dice and games, playing on alternate days so they could endure the hunger.
greek_mythology.explanation: A whole people held on to their games, and to life, through years of suffering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Clinging to play and to life amid hardship echoes both halves of the Kural's comparison.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Summarised from the well-known passage but not re-checked verbatim this session; a loose thematic parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Not that there is in fact any happiness in them, or that men imagine true bliss to consist in money won at play, or in the hare which they hunt; we would not take these as a gift. ... Reasons why we like the chase better than the quarry.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal observes that gamblers do not really want the winnings; they want the play itself, the chase rather than the prize.
philosophy.tie_back: That is why, as the Kural says, losing only deepens the gambler's love for the game.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)
